title: Insurance deduction has tax trap
full_text:
SMSF members electing to use the future service deduction (FSD) for life insurance premiums paid from their fund should be aware this process may also pass a tax liability to a beneficiary, according to a sector educator.
Heffron senior SMSF education specialist Natasha Panagis said under the FSD instead of claiming deductions for premiums each year, a member can elect to claim a single larger deduction when a benefit is paid based on any future service days, such as up to the member’s expected retirement date, that would be covered by the policy.
However, Panagis noted there were key drawbacks for the member and their beneficiaries in making this choice.
“We don’t generally see the FSD used in practice. The reason is because the choice is permanent. Once you make the choice to claim the deduction, it means any future premiums for existing members and those who join the fund later won’t be deductible,” she said during a recent presentation for The Auditors Institute.
“Once you’ve made the choice, you set that in stone and can’t change your deduction method going forward.
“Looking at other downsides depends on who your beneficiaries are, and while the deduction sounds great, we need to think about if an untaxed element of a lump sum death benefit may arise.
“That can occur where the member dies before the age of 65, the insurance was still in force at the time of death, the death benefit is paid as a lump sum to a non-death benefits dependant or a non-tax dependant, and the fund has claimed an insurance-related deduction either through an insurance premium deduction or through the FSD.
“Where any of these conditions are met, part of the taxable component is going to be reclassified as an untaxed element in the fund and that’s going to be subject to a higher rate of tax [of 30 per cent] when paid to the beneficiary.
“While claiming the deduction can be a valuable tax saving for the SMSF today, it’s important to consider the potential cost for beneficiaries in the future.
“If you just had a spouse, that wouldn’t be a problem, but if a member’s super is likely to pass to a non-tax dependant, such as an independent adult child, it might be worthwhile considering whether insurance deductions should be claimed at all.
“It is worthwhile weighing up that immediate tax saving for the SMSF against the future potential tax cost for the beneficiaries.”
author: Jason Spits
